column4: Welcome to options. Here is the single idea everything else rests on: an option is a contract that gives you the right, but never the obligation, to buy or sell something at a set price. You are buying a choice, not a promise to act. Over the next few minutes you will meet calls and puts, break down the three parts of every contract, and get a plain-language feel for the Greeks. Press start and let's open it up.

Options come in two flavors, and the whole game starts here. A call is the right to buy the underlying at an agreed price. You buy calls when you think the price is heading up. A put is the right to sell the underlying at that agreed price. You buy puts when you think the price is heading down. Look at the split on screen: a green arrow rising for the call, a red arrow falling for the put. Both are derivative contracts, which just means their value comes from something else, the stock or asset sitting underneath them.

Every option contract has three moving parts. The strike is the agreed price you can buy or sell at. The expiration is the deadline, the date the contract stops existing. And the premium is what you pay to own that right. That premium splits into two pieces: intrinsic value, the part that is real money right now, and time value, what you pay for the chance the price moves your way before expiration. Two ideas to hold onto. Options give you leverage, so a smaller amount of capital can control a larger position. And when you buy an option, the most you can lose is the premium you paid, nothing beyond it. Glance at the three pill cards. Delta is sensitivity to direction. Theta is time decay. Vega is sensitivity to volatility. That is your Greeks-lite starter kit.

column3: In or Out of the Money
column4: So is your option worth something right now, or not yet? That question has a name: moneyness. A call is in-the-money when the price sits above the strike, because you would rather buy low while the market trades higher. A put is in-the-money when the price sits below the strike, because you would rather sell high than at the lower market. Out-of-the-money is simply the opposite in each case. In-the-money options carry intrinsic value, real worth baked in today. Out-of-the-money options are all time value and hope.

Your turn. Drag the stock price up and down against the fixed strike line and watch the two badges flip. When the price climbs above the strike, the call lights up green, in-the-money, and the put goes grey. Push the price below the strike and it reverses. Play with it until the pattern feels automatic, because reading moneyness at a glance is half the battle. The numbers here are illustrative, just the shape of the idea, not a forecast or a promise.

Let's make sure calls and puts really stick. Sort these cards yourself. Tap a card to pick it up, then drop it under Buy a Call if it points to a bullish, price-rising view, or under Buy a Put if it points to a bearish, price-falling view. Think about direction every time. Bullish leans toward calls, bearish leans toward puts.
Five quick questions to lock it in. Take your time and answer to earn your points for the lesson.

Let's gather the four ideas. A call is the right to buy, a put is the right to sell, and both are contracts, never obligations. Every option carries a strike, an expiration, and a premium. In-the-money means real intrinsic value, out-of-the-money is all time and hope. And delta, theta, and vega tell you how a contract reacts to direction, time, and volatility. Next up is lesson four point two, buying options on a thesis without blowing up. We will turn this vocabulary into a careful, risk-aware play.
